title: Knowledge check: Switch Statements

questions.prompt: For “Switch Statements”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Switch Statements is one step in Conditions, Loops, and Control Flow; branches select paths; loops repeat work. Guard clauses and well-defined exit conditions prevent fragile logic. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Switch Statements” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Using switch()” as part of lesson 52. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Switch Statements” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Test typical, boundary, empty, and missing inputs. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
